items.title: Your Phone Can Spot Undercover Cop Cars for You Using WiFi and Bluetooth
items.summary:
Seems like we’re all under surveillance in 2026, which makes me all the more eager to boost my own situational awareness wherever I can. Radar detectors help, but they only work when you’re in the sights of specific tracking tools. This new Android app, called SØPHIA, looks like it could be a great supplement, using the Wi-Fi and Bluetooth radios your phone already has to watch the watchers.

SØPHIA caught our attention as it’s been making the rounds on Instagram . The developer pitches it as a “wireless awareness tool,” and lists its main features thusly:

See what’s nearby: Observe Wi-Fi networks and Bluetooth devices in real time. 

Spot interesting signals: Built-in classifications highlight supported equipment and infrastructure. 

Watch what matters: Save identifiers, network names, or keywords to your Watchlist and receive visual and optional audio alerts when they appear again. 

Filter the noise: Mute signals you don’t want generating alerts. 

Review your findings: Export observations as CSV or JSON, or prepare an AI Debrief for further analysis. 

There are a few demos of different use cases on the Sophia_Ops YouTube channel . Basically, the program works like a radar for anything that emits a signal. Because it matches those signals to known identifiers, it can give you a live feed of the connected devices nearby.

items.title: Scout CEO Promises a Real Service Network, Even With Direct Sales
items.summary:
As Scout Motors prepares for full-blown production at its newly built South Carolina plant, the startup automaker keeps fighting dealer drama — and plenty of it . Much of it traces back to the Volkswagen Group’s ownership of Scout. See, VW stores want to sell and service these adventurous 4x4s because that’s what people are buying in droves, but the brand’s leadership has made it clear : That ain’t happenin’. Scout is planning a mix of online and in-person retail sales, and as Scout CEO Scott Keogh explained to us on an episode of The Drivecast , owners won’t be left hanging when it comes to service.

Talk of a digital sales experience has been met with mumbles and mutters such as, “Who will maintain these fancified electric four-wheelers? What about warranty work?” And to that, Keogh told us, “Look. One-hundred percent, we are going to service the vehicle.”

“I think there’s a myth out there. The myth is: If we go direct to consumer, that means it’s a mobile app digital thing, and we’re just going to abandon you and be a digital enterprise. No, no,” Keogh continued. “We’re also going to do serious hardware, and that hardware manifests itself as we’re going to build a hundred Scout stores in the country, and those Scout stores are going to have lifts, they’re going to have technicians, and they’re going to fix your car. You’re going to go to them to do test drives, and you’re going to go to them to service your vehicle.”

items.title: Scout CEO Says Company Is ‘Structured’ to Go Public, If It Wants

However, the revival brand also has big plans on the business side, recently telling us it  could  go public if it wanted to.

When asked if Volkswagen Group leadership would consider outside investment so people could own a piece of Scout, Keogh said that the company is “structured for that possibility.”

“We always structured Scout from day one to be completely independent,” Keogh told The Drive . “We’re a separate, consolidated [entity] in Delaware and reporting directly to Germany. So we structured it to be capable of taking on strategic investors to potentially invest in the company over time, and potentially go to capital markets and go to an IPO. This is not confirming that we’re doing that, to be clear, but we always structured the company for that possibility.”

items.title: 2026 Chevrolet Corvette ZR1 Review: The Sum of All Dreams
items.summary:
In any conversation about the cars that captivated us as kids, the Ford GT90 will forever be my pick. Nothing about it looked organic or the product of human thought. It had 720 horsepower back in 1995, when that was a lot of horsepower, thanks to four turbochargers that, as Need for Speed II players know, rushed exhaust gases so volcanically hot they’d melt ordinary body panels, forcing Ford to fit ceramic tiles normally used for space travel. It really was otherworldly. And, unlike today’s concept cars, it actually worked.

Still, you can’t drive it; even the keeper of the lone example can’t really drive it because, I mean, how could anyone? It’s a gleaming, one-of-one monument to 20th-century American engineering. The good news is that, while it took about 30 years, today there is actually a Ford GT90 you can drive, only more modern and less rare. It’s called the Chevrolet Corvette ZR1, and it is perfect.

The Corvette ZR1 represents excess in every respect. Its 5.5-liter, twin-turbocharged, LT7 flat-plane-crank V8 makes 1,064 horsepower and 828 lb-ft of torque, sent through an eight-speed dual-clutch gearbox to the rear wheels alone. Because the only Vette that the ZR1 answers to is the 1,250-hp, hybrid, all-wheel-drive ZR1X.

On Thursday at the 2026 Los Angeles Auto Show, Senior Vice President and Chief Planning Officer for Nissan North America, Ponz Pandikuthira, exclusively told The Drive , “No, I don’t think so” when asked if the next GT-R needs a retro design or horizontal headlights and R34-esque elements while also saying the car could blend retro and modern design cues.

“Now, many things need to be refined and they don’t need to lock down the design of a car in 2026 for a 2030 or 2031 production. Not at all,” Pandikuthira said.

That timeline lines up with what Pandikuthira told The Drive in April when also revealing the hybridized powertrain will utilize the VR38 block.

GT-Rs, especially the last-gen, the R35 model, have long shelf lives. This impacts the design as it has to stand the test of time. “So there’d be a lot of work in progress to see how it evolves. I do not expect the car to be purely retro, where it just looks old. It needs to look new and needs to have life. This previous, uh, generation, the R35 lasted from 2007 till 2024. So let’s, let’s come up with a car that can live for a long time without anything that’s just polarizing and retro that doesn’t look cool after six years,” Pandikuthira noted.

items.title: Hyundai N Vision 74 Production Plans Are Dead, For Now
items.summary:
Hyundai’s N Vision 74 ground the automotive internet to a halt on a Friday in July four years ago. With that concept, the automaker recast one of the most consequential models of its history, the Giugiaro-penned, 1974 Pony, into a modern supercar with turbofans and an unapologetically big wing. Enthusiasts have waited to see it get the green light for production ever since. To hear a Hyundai executive tell it, that ship has likely already sailed.

Rumblings have come and gone, and reports of trademark renewals have kept a glimmer of hope alive, but the beat has gone cold. For unfortunately good reason, as Hyundai Design Center boss Simon Loasby explained to The Drive during the media preview for the 2027 Elantra . We asked him if the N Vision 74 would ever get produced, and his answer was predictable, but nevertheless disappointing.

“At the moment, no,” Loasby said. “We were really on it. We had the production clay model of it and the exterior, interior, and so on. It comes down to the maths of how you judge what the business case is. And that if you’re very tight with the business case on only that car, the volumes of that car and the impact, you got no chance. If you open it to the overall brand-raising profile value of that, you have a bigger chance. But as yet, [no].”

items.title: Here’s Why Scout Isn’t Doing Removable Doors and Roofs Yet
items.summary:
Scout might be staking its claim as the electric truck brand for serious off-roaders and explorers who need ladder-frame power and dependability, but it’s not necessarily angling to replace the Wrangler and Bronco on their turf.

During his appearance on The Drivecast , Scout CEO Scott Keogh said that removable doors and roof panels are not something the revived brand is planning—at least, not yet.

“We’ve been interacting with the Scout community—actually, we showed the first concept to the Scout OGs before we showed the journalists,” Keogh said. “We invited them down to Dallas, and look—the number one thing we wanted to do was build an authentic, credible, rugged vehicle. Hence body-on-frame, hence solid rear axle, hence mechanical switches and door handles, all those kind of things. So, 100% we’ve achieved that. We will not do removable doors and removable tops on the Traveler as we know it.”

Scout Motors 

Keogh said if Scout props up another model, a three-row SUV would be a likely candidate. Given that, the potential for a more modular SUV with optional panels, in the vein of the Wrangler and Bronco, seems like a far-off consideration. But he didn’t shut the door.

“Is there some future we would look at that type of vehicle? 100%,” Keogh added. “For the Traveler and for this Terra, no. Why did we make that decision? If you look at the application and the market and everything we wanted to achieve, this is the best way achieving it—the vehicle that you’re seeing right here, without a doubt.”

Ampudia and Australian co-driver Paul Weel brought Team Papas’ No. 1 Trophy Truck into San José del Cabo early on Saturday, November 14, 13.5 seconds ahead of Bryce Menzies and Andy McMillin in the No. 7 on raw time. When SCORE International posted corrected results on Sunday, Menzies and McMillin had won by 1 minute, 38 seconds.

The swing came from a timing adjustment to one speed-zone section north of Loreto. Ampudia says it cost him a win he earned by following the rules. Fans are divided on the strength of his case, and even the winners aren’t fully celebrating.
